phy_ocrb.4.1.summary: This chapter explores the subatomic structure of atoms, focusing on protons, neutrons, and electrons, and how they define elements and isotopes. Students must master nuclear notation using atomic and mass numbers to represent different isotopes precisely. Understanding these foundational building blocks is essential for analyzing nuclear radiation, decays, and reactions later in GCSE Physics.

core.p: Atoms are the fundamental building blocks of all matter, consisting of a central nucleus surrounded by orbiting electrons in energy levels. The nucleus is extremely small compared to the overall size of the atom, yet it contains virtually all of the atom's mass.
bullets: Atoms have a radius of approximately 1 x 10^-10 metres (0.1 nanometres).
The nucleus has a radius of about 1 x 10^-14 metres, which is about 10,000 times smaller than the atom.
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively known as nucleons.
Electrons orbit the nucleus in discrete energy levels or shells at specific distances.

callouts.p: The tiny, dense central core of an atom composed of protons and neutrons, carrying a positive charge.
Because the nucleus is 10,000 times smaller than the atom, an atom is mostly empty space.

fig.cap: Diagram showing the relative scale of an atom and its tiny central nucleus.

core.h: 2. Subatomic Particles: Protons, Neutrons and Electrons
core.p: Subatomic particles are distinguished by their relative masses and relative electrical charges. These properties determine both the chemical identity of an atom and its stability.
bullets: Protons have a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of +1.
Neutrons have a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of 0 (neutral).
Electrons have a very small relative mass (approx 1/1836 or 0.0005) and a relative charge of -1.
In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, balancing the overall charge to zero.

callouts.p: Never say electrons have 'no mass'; state they have a 'negligible' or 'very small' mass.

core.p: Every element is defined by the number of protons in its nucleus. The total count of protons and neutrons gives the overall mass of the nucleus.
bullets: Atomic number (proton number, Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Mass number (nucleon number, A) is the total number of protons and neutrons combined in the nucleus.
Number of neutrons = Mass number (A) minus Atomic number (Z).
The atomic number determines which chemical element the atom is.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

core.p: Physicists use a standard notation format to represent nuclides clearly, showing both the chemical symbol and the numerical values for mass and atomic numbers.
bullets: The chemical symbol of the element is written in the centre (e.g., C for carbon, U for uranium).
The mass number (A) is written as a superscript at the top left of the chemical symbol.
The atomic number (Z) is written as a subscript at the bottom left of the chemical symbol.
Example: Carbon-14 is written as 14-C with 6 at the bottom left.

callouts.p: A over Z next to X: Superscript A is total nucleons, subscript Z is protons.

fig.cap: Standard nuclear notation breakdown showing mass number A and atomic number Z.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><text x="200" y="110" text-anchor="middle" font-size="48" fill="#1b2540">X</text><text x="150" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="#2563eb">A</text><text x="150" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="#16a34a">Z</text><line x1="165" y1="85" x2="185" y2="100" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="165" y1="130" x2="185" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="200" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">A = Mass number (Protons + Neutrons)</text><text x="200" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Z = Atomic number (Protons only)</text></svg>

core.p: Not all atoms of the same element are identical. Variations in the number of neutrons lead to the existence of isotopes.
bullets: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Because they have the same number of protons, isotopes have identical chemical properties.
Because they have different numbers of neutrons, isotopes have different mass numbers and different physical properties (such as nuclear stability and mass).
Many isotopes are radioactive because their nuclei are unstable.

callouts.p: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes react chemically in the exact same way because chemical reactions depend on electrons, not neutrons.

core.h: 6. Examples of Isotopes: Hydrogen and Carbon
core.p: Exam questions frequently use hydrogen and carbon to test understanding of isotopes, nucleon calculations, and nuclear symbols.
bullets: Hydrogen has three common isotopes: Protium (1-H-1), Deuterium (2-H-1), and Tritium (3-H-1).
Protium has 1 proton and 0 neutrons.
Deuterium has 1 proton and 1 neutron.
Tritium has 1 proton and 2 neutrons (and is radioactive).
Carbon has stable isotopes Carbon-12 and Carbon-13, and the radioactive isotope Carbon-14.

callouts.p: Protium is the only stable nuclide known that has zero neutrons in its nucleus.

fig.cap: Comparison of the three isotopes of hydrogen showing varying neutron counts.

core.h: 7. Calculating Subatomic Particles from Nuclear Notation
core.p: Given any nuclide in standard notation, you must be able to determine the exact count of protons, neutrons, and electrons immediately.
bullets: Number of protons = Subscript Z.
Number of electrons = Subscript Z (assuming a neutral atom with no charge).
Number of neutrons = Superscript A minus Subscript Z.
Example: For Uranium-235 (235-U with 92 at the bottom): Protons = 92, Electrons = 92, Neutrons = 235 - 92 = 143.

callouts.p: Always double-check your subtraction for neutrons: A - Z. Students often mistakenly subtract the other way or add them together.

core.p: It is vital not to confuse isotopes with ions. While isotopes vary in neutrons, ions vary in electrons due to the gain or loss of charge.
bullets: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained one or more electrons, resulting in a net electrical charge.
Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons; ions have different numbers of electrons.
Isotopes of the same element still have identical atomic numbers (Z).
Ions of the same element still have identical atomic numbers and mass numbers, only the electron shell count differs.

callouts.p: Do not mix up ions (charged atoms due to electron transfer) with isotopes (atoms with different neutron counts).

core.p: The ratio of neutrons to protons within a nucleus dictates whether that isotope is stable or unstable (radioactive).
bullets: Light elements (like Carbon and Oxygen) are most stable when the neutron-to-proton ratio is approximately 1:1.
Heavier elements (like Uranium and Radium) require progressively more neutrons than protons to bind the nucleus together against electrostatic repulsion.
If a nucleus has too many or too few neutrons, it is unstable.
Unstable isotopes undergo radioactive decay to achieve a more stable configuration.

callouts.p: Unstable isotopes emit ionising radiation (alpha, beta, gamma, or neutrons) to become stable.

core.p: In nuclear equations, standard notation is used for all reactants and products to ensure that both mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.
bullets: The sum of mass numbers (superscripts) on the left must equal the sum on the right.
The sum of atomic numbers (subscripts) on the left must equal the sum on the right.
Every particle involved, including alpha particles (4-He-2) and beta particles (0-e--1), uses nuclear notation.
Balancing nuclear equations relies directly on correct interpretation of mass and atomic numbers.

callouts.p: Nucleon number and total charge are always conserved in any nuclear reaction.

analogy.p: Imagine books in a library. The subject genre (e.g., Physics, History) is like the atomic number (Z)—it defines what kind of book it is and what is inside. The total number of pages in the book is like the mass number (A). Two books might be on the exact same subject with the exact same number of pages, but one might have an extra appendix chapter of notes added at the back; this extra chapter represents extra neutrons, making it an isotope. Where this analogy breaks down is that books don't spontaneously eject pages to become stable, whereas unstable atomic nuclei do emit radiation.

terms.d: The smallest neutral particle of a chemical element that retains its chemical properties.
The tiny, dense, positively charged central core of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of +1.
A subatomic particle found in the nucleus with a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of 0.
A subatomic particle orbiting the nucleus with a very small relative mass and a relative charge of -1.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, defining the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons combined in the nucleus of an atom.
A particle located in the nucleus; either a proton or a neutron.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A specific type of atom characterized by a given number of protons and neutrons.
An atom or molecule that has gained or lost one or more electrons, giving it a net electrical charge.
An isotope with an unstable nucleus that decays, emitting ionising radiation to become more stable.

mistakes.w: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the SAME number of protons; they differ in the number of neutrons.

mistakes.w: Stating that electrons have zero mass.
mistakes.r: Electrons have a very small or negligible mass (about 1/1836 of a proton), not zero.

mistakes.w: Subtracting atomic number from mass number to find electrons.
mistakes.r: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the atomic number (Z), not A - Z.

mistakes.w: Confusing mass number with atomic number in nuclear notation.
mistakes.r: Mass number (A) is always the top number (superscript); atomic number (Z) is always the bottom number (subscript).

mistakes.w: Claiming isotopes have different chemical properties.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have identical chemical properties because chemical reactivity depends entirely on electron configuration.

mistakes.w: Writing ions when the question asks about isotopes.
mistakes.r: Ions involve changes in electrons; isotopes involve changes in neutrons.

mistakes.w: Stating that the nucleus takes up most of the atom's volume.
mistakes.r: The atom is mostly empty space; the nucleus is 10,000 times smaller than the atom.

exam.q: Define the term 'isotopes' in terms of subatomic particles.
model: Atoms of the same element / same number of protons
With different numbers of neutrons
exam.tip: Both points are required for full marks. Never say 'different number of electrons'.

exam.q: An atom of carbon is represented as 14-C with 6 at the bottom. State the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in this atom.
model: Protons = 6
Electrons = 6
Neutrons = 8 (14 - 6)
exam.tip: Subtract the subscript from the superscript to find neutrons.

exam.q: Explain why isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties.
model: They have the same number of protons
So they have the same number of electrons and identical electron configuration
exam.tip: Chemical reactions depend on electrons, so link protons to electrons.

exam.q: Compare the relative mass and relative charge of a proton and a neutron.
model: Both have the same relative mass of 1
Proton has a relative charge of +1 whereas neutron has a relative charge of 0
exam.tip: State both similarities and differences clearly.

exam.q: State the location and approximate relative size of the nucleus compared to the whole atom.
model: Located at the centre of the atom
About 10,000 times smaller than the atom / radius is 10^-14 m compared to 10^-10 m
exam.tip: Include both the scale factor and position for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why some isotopes are radioactive.
model: They have unstable nuclei
Due to an unbalanced or unsuitable ratio of neutrons to protons
exam.tip: Mention nuclear stability and neutron-proton imbalance.

exam.q: Sodium-23 (23-Na with 11 at the bottom) forms a Sodium ion (Na+) by losing one electron. State the number of protons and electrons in this ion.
model: Protons = 11
Electrons = 10
exam.tip: Remember that a positive ion has lost one electron from the neutral count.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a nucleon number and a proton number.
model: Proton number is just the number of protons (Z)
Nucleon number is the total sum of protons and neutrons (A)
exam.tip: Use the alternative terms Z and A to ensure precision.

exam.q: State what is meant by a 'nuclide'.
model: A specific type of atom or nucleus with a defined number of protons and neutrons
exam.tip: Keep definitions concise and learn them word for word.

exam.q: A neutral atom has 92 protons and 143 neutrons. Write its standard nuclear notation.
model: Mass number = 92 + 143 = 235 (superscript)
Atomic number = 92 (subscript) with symbol U
exam.tip: Calculate the mass number first by adding protons and neutrons.

worked.q: Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in the neutral chlorine isotope written as 37-Cl with 17 at the bottom.
steps: Identify the atomic number (Z) from the subscript: Z = 17. This is the number of protons.
Recognize that in a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Therefore, electrons = 17.
Identify the mass number (A) from the superscript: A = 37.
Calculate the number of neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number: Neutrons = 37 - 17 = 20.

worked.q: Two neutral atoms are represented as 12-C (with 6 at the bottom) and 13-C (with 6 at the bottom). Explain why these are isotopes and state one similarity and one difference in their atomic structure.
steps: Check atomic numbers: both have Z = 6, meaning they have the same number of protons and are the same element (carbon).
Check mass numbers: one has A = 12 and the other has A = 13, meaning they have different neutron counts (12 - 6 = 6 neutrons vs 13 - 6 = 7 neutrons).
Conclude definition: because they have the same proton number but different neutron numbers, they are isotopes.
State similarity: both have 6 protons (and 6 electrons).
State difference: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons while Carbon-13 has 7 neutrons.
worked.ans: They are isotopes because they have the same proton number (6) but different neutron numbers (6 and 7 respectively). Similarity: both have 6 protons. Difference: different number of neutrons.

phy_ocrb.4.4.summary: This topic covers the properties of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation regarding their penetration through various materials and their interaction with matter. It distinguishes clearly between irradiation (exposure to radiation without physical contact with the source) and radioactive contamination (the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside materials), which is crucial for safety and protection in medical, industrial, and research settings.

core.h: Introduction to Penetration and Ionising Power
core.p: When radioactive isotopes decay, they emit ionising radiation. The type of radiation emitted determines how deeply it can penetrate materials and how strongly it ionises atoms along its path.
bullets: Ionisation involves stripping electrons from neutral atoms to form charged ions.
The three main types of ionising radiation are alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays.
There is an inverse relationship between a radiation type's ionising power and its penetrating power.
High ionising power means energy is transferred to matter quickly, stopping the radiation sooner.

callouts.p: The more ionising a radiation type is, the less deeply it penetrates.

core.p: Alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons, identical to a helium nucleus. Because they are relatively heavy and carry a double positive charge, they interact strongly with matter.
bullets: Range in air: only a few centimetres (about 5 cm).
Stopped by: a single sheet of paper or the outer layer of human skin.
Ionising power: very high due to large mass and +2 charge.
Deflected by electric and magnetic fields because of their positive charge.

callouts.p: A fast-moving helium nucleus consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

core.p: Beta particles are high-speed electrons emitted from the nucleus when a neutron decays into a proton. They are much smaller and lighter than alpha particles.
bullets: Range in air: about 1 metre.
Stopped by: a thin sheet of aluminium (around 3 mm thick).
Ionising power: moderate (lower than alpha, higher than gamma).
Deflected by electric and magnetic fields due to their negative charge.

callouts.p: A high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus during radioactive decay.

core.p: Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves emitted from the nucleus. Having no mass and no charge, they interact much less frequently with matter.
bullets: Range in air: unlimited (follows an inverse square law for intensity).
Stopped by: thick lead or thick concrete.
Ionising power: low because they pass straight through most atoms without interacting.
Not deflected by electric or magnetic fields as they are uncharged.

callouts.p: High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.

core.p: Exam questions frequently require comparing the three types of ionising radiation across multiple physical characteristics.
bullets: Alpha: Helium nucleus, +2 charge, very high ionising, stopped by paper.
Beta: Fast electron, -1 charge, moderate ionising, stopped by aluminium.
Gamma: EM wave, 0 charge, low ionising, reduced by thick lead.

callouts.p: Commit this table to memory; comparison questions are worth 3 to 4 marks.

core.p: Irradiation is the process by which an object is exposed to ionising radiation. Crucially, the irradiated object does not become radioactive itself.
bullets: The radiation source is external to the object being irradiated.
Exposure stops the moment the source is removed or shielded.
Used for sterilising medical equipment and preserving food.
Lead aprons or concrete barriers are used to protect workers from irradiation.

callouts.p: The process of exposing an object to ionising radiation; the object does not become radioactive.

core.p: Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside other materials. This poses a sustained hazard because the source is now in direct contact with or inside the object.
bullets: The contaminating material will continue to emit radiation as long as it remains present.
Can occur externally (skin or clothes) or internally (inhaled or ingested).
Alpha emitters are extremely hazardous if ingested because they are highly ionising to internal tissue.
Decontamination requires washing, removing clothing, or surgical removal.

callouts.p: The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials.

core.p: Understanding the difference between irradiation and contamination is vital for assessing risks and implementing proper safety measures.
bullets: Irradiation source is outside; contamination source is in/on the body.
Irradiation stops when shielding is applied; contamination persists until the radioactive isotope is removed or decays.
Contamination hazards depend heavily on the type of radiation emitted (alpha inside the body is most dangerous).

callouts.p: Do not confuse the two! Irradiation is exposure to rays; contamination is getting radioactive dust or liquid on/in you.

core.p: To protect against the hazards of ionising radiation, specific handling procedures and safety measures are enforced in all laboratories and medical facilities.
bullets: Time: Minimise the time spent near radioactive sources.
Distance: Use tongs or robotic arms to increase distance from sources (inverse square law reduces dose).
Shielding: Use lead screens for gamma, lab coats and safety specs for beta/alpha.
Monitoring: Wear film badges or Geiger-Muller counters to track cumulative dose.

callouts.p: Radiation doses must be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

core.p: A standard required or demonstration practical involves using a Geiger-Muller (GM) tube and counter to measure the penetration of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation through different absorbers.
bullets: Step 1: Measure background count rate with no source present.
Step 2: Place a radioactive source near the GM tube and record the count rate.
Step 3: Insert a paper sheet between source and tube; if count drops to background level, the source is alpha.
Step 4: Insert aluminium sheet; if count drops, it is beta. If it passes through, it is gamma.

callouts.p: Always subtract the background count rate from your measured readings to get the correct corrected count rate.

fig.cap: Experimental setup for testing radiation penetration using a GM tube and absorbers.

core.h: Higher Tier: Electric and Magnetic Deflection
core.p: Because alpha and beta particles are charged, their trajectories are bent by electric and magnetic fields in opposite directions due to their opposite charges.
bullets: Alpha particles have a +2 charge and are deflected less than beta particles due to their much greater mass.
Beta particles have a -1 charge and are deflected significantly in the opposite direction to alpha particles.
Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves and pass straight through fields without any deflection.
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule or charge force rules determine the direction of deflection.

callouts.p: Alpha and beta deflect oppositely; gamma does not deflect at all.

analogy.p: Imagine alpha particles as heavy paintballs (stopped by cardboard/paper), beta particles as small metal BB pellets (stopped by a thin sheet of metal), and gamma rays as intense laser beams (requiring thick concrete or lead walls to block). Irradiation is like standing near a spotlight (you are illuminated, but no light sticks to you), whereas contamination is like spilling wet paint on your clothes (the paint is on you and continues to make a mess until washed off).

terms.d: A particle consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, identical to a helium nucleus, with a +2 charge.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus during radioactive decay, with a -1 charge.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the atomic nucleus.
The ability of radiation to pass through different thicknesses of materials.
The ability of radiation to knock electrons out of atoms to create ions.
The process of exposing an object to ionising radiation without making it radioactive.
The unwanted presence of radioactive substances on or in other materials.
A detector used to measure the count rate of ionising radiation.
Low-level ionising radiation present around us all the time from natural and artificial sources.
The measured count rate minus the background count rate.
Materials placed between a radiation source and living tissue or equipment to absorb radiation.
A material used in experiments to test the penetrating properties of different types of radiation.

mistakes.w: Stating that irradiation makes an object radioactive.
mistakes.r: Irradiation exposes an object to radiation, but the object itself does not become radioactive.

mistakes.w: Confusing the range of alpha and gamma in air (saying gamma travels a few cm).
mistakes.r: Alpha travels a few cm in air; gamma has an effectively unlimited range (following an inverse square law).

mistakes.w: Saying beta particles are orbiting electrons.
mistakes.r: Beta particles originate from the nucleus when a neutron decays into a proton.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to subtract background radiation in experiments.
mistakes.r: Always state that background count rate must be measured and subtracted from all readings.

mistakes.w: Describing contamination as radiation being shone on someone.
mistakes.r: Contamination is physical contact with or ingestion/inhalation of radioactive atoms.

mistakes.w: Believing gamma rays have a positive charge.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves.

mistakes.w: Stating alpha is stopped by aluminium.
mistakes.r: Alpha is stopped by paper/skin; aluminium stops beta particles.

exam.q: State the difference between irradiation and contamination.
model: Irradiation is exposure to radiation without physical contact with the source
Contamination is the presence of radioactive atoms on or inside an object
exam.tip: Make sure to contrast source location or radioactive status.

exam.q: Explain why an alpha source in a sealed plastic box is safe to handle, but dangerous if swallowed.
model: Alpha particles have a very short range and are stopped by thin plastic or skin
Outside the body, alpha cannot reach internal cells
If swallowed, alpha radiation is directly in contact with internal tissue and is highly ionising, causing severe damage
exam.tip: Mention both range/shielding externally and internal ionising hazard.

exam.q: Describe how you would use an aluminium sheet to determine if a radioactive source emits beta radiation.
model: Measure the initial count rate using a GM tube without the aluminium sheet
Place the aluminium sheet between the source and the GM tube
If the count rate drops significantly (or to background levels), beta radiation is present
exam.tip: Always include measuring count rate before and after adding the absorber.

exam.q: Compare the ionising power and penetrating power of alpha and gamma radiation.
model: Alpha has high ionising power, whereas gamma has low ionising power
Alpha has low penetrating power and is stopped by paper
Gamma has high penetrating power and requires thick lead to reduce intensity
Ionising power is inversely proportional to penetrating power
exam.tip: Cover both ionising and penetrating aspects for both types.

exam.q: Explain why background radiation must be accounted for when measuring the count rate of a radioactive source.
model: Background radiation is always present from natural and artificial sources
Subtracting background ensures readings measure only radiation from the source
exam.tip: Keep it concise: background is constant ambient radiation that must be removed.

exam.q: A student measures a count rate of 340 counts per minute (cpm) with a beta source and an aluminium absorber of 3 mm. The background count rate is 40 cpm. Calculate the corrected count rate.
model: Corrected count rate = Measured count rate - Background count rate
exam.tip: Always state the formula and show your subtraction clearly.

exam.q: Explain why gamma emitting sources are used for medical tracing inside the body.
model: Gamma rays have high penetration so they can pass out of the body to be detected
Gamma has low ionising power, minimising tissue damage compared to alpha
exam.tip: Link properties (penetration and low ionisation) to medical application.

exam.q: Describe what happens to a beta particle when it passes through an electric field.
model: Beta particles carry a negative charge
They are deflected towards the positive plate of the electric field
exam.tip: Remember opposite charges attract.

exam.q: Give two safety precautions a scientist should take when handling a gamma ray source.
model: Use tongs to maintain distance from the source
Keep exposure time as short as possible / use lead shielding
exam.tip: Time, distance, and shielding are the three golden rules of radiation safety.

worked.q: A student investigates a radioactive source. With no source, the GM counter reads 25 cpm. With the source and no absorbers, the count is 425 cpm. With paper, the count is 420 cpm. With 3 mm aluminium, the count is 30 cpm. Identify the type(s) of radiation emitted.
steps: Calculate corrected background-free count rates for each condition.
Initial corrected count = 425 - 25 = 400 cpm.
With paper, corrected count = 420 - 25 = 395 cpm (virtually no reduction; alpha is not present or is negligible).
With aluminium, corrected count = 30 - 25 = 5 cpm (drops back to background level).
Conclusion: The source emits beta radiation because aluminium stops it while paper does not.

worked.q: Explain why handling an open alpha source with bare hands is dangerous even if gloves are worn, whereas handling a sealed gamma source with tongs is relatively safe.
steps: Identify contamination risk: An open alpha source can transfer radioactive dust onto skin or hands (contamination).
Assess alpha hazard inside/on the body: Alpha is highly ionising and dangerous if contamination occurs.
Identify irradiation risk: A sealed gamma source emits penetrating rays that reach the body from a distance (irradiation).
Apply distance protection: Using tongs increases distance, obeying the inverse square law to reduce the dose significantly.
worked.ans: Open alpha causes internal/external contamination which is highly ionising; sealed gamma poses irradiation risk which is mitigated by increasing distance with tongs.

phy_ocrb.4.5.summary: This topic covers the critical medical applications of ionising radiation in diagnosis and treatment, alongside the essential differences between irradiation and contamination. It explores the biological hazards of ionising radiation on living tissue and DNA, and requires precise calculations and graphical interpretation of radioactive half-life to determine activity and safe handling periods.

core.h: Penetration Properties of Alpha, Beta, and Gamma
core.p: Different types of ionising radiation have vastly different penetrating powers and ranges in matter, which directly dictates how they are used in medicine and how safely they can be handled.
bullets: **Alpha particles ($\alpha$)**: Highly ionising, consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus). Range in air is only a few centimetres; stopped by a single sheet of paper or human skin.
**Beta particles ($\beta$)**: Moderately ionising, consisting of fast-moving electrons emitted from the nucleus. Range in air is about 1 metre; stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
**Gamma rays ($\gamma$)**: Weakly ionising electromagnetic waves of high frequency. Range in air is virtually unlimited (inverse square law applies); stopped only by thick lead or metres of concrete.
Penetration depends strictly on mass, charge, and the probability of interacting with atomic electrons in the material traversed.

callouts.p: Never confuse ionising power with penetrating power: they are inversely related. Alpha is most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is least ionising but most penetrating.

core.p: Students must clearly distinguish between being exposed to radiation from an external source and actually having radioactive material physically present inside or on the body.
bullets: **Irradiation**: The process of exposing an object to ionising radiation. The irradiated object does **not** become radioactive. Exposure stops as soon as the source is removed or shielded.
**Contamination**: The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside other materials. The contaminated object remains radioactive for as long as the source is present and decaying.
Medical equipment is often **sterilised** by irradiation using gamma rays so that microbes are killed without the equipment becoming radioactive itself.
Contamination hazards depend heavily on whether the radioactive material is ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through wounds into living tissue.

callouts.p: Irradiation is the exposure of a material to ionising radiation; it does not make the material radioactive.
Contamination is the transfer of radioactive material onto or into an object, causing the object to be radioactive.

core.h: Hazards of Ionising Radiation on Living Tissue
core.p: Ionising radiation strips electrons from atoms, creating reactive ions that break chemical bonds and damage living cells.
bullets: Radiation can ionise molecules within human cells, most notably **DNA**, leading to cell death or dangerous genetic mutations.
Mutated DNA can cause cells to divide uncontrollably, resulting in cancerous tumours.
High doses of radiation cause acute radiation sickness, burns, organ failure, and rapid death.
Low doses over time increase the long-term statistical risk of developing cancer.

callouts.p: Radiation does not make your whole body radioactive when you are irradiated externally. It only damages cells directly via ionisation.

core.p: Working safely with radioactive sources requires strict adherence to control measures designed to minimise exposure time, maximise distance, and use appropriate physical shielding.
bullets: **Time**: Minimise the time spent handling or standing near radioactive sources.
**Distance**: Increase the distance between yourself and the source. Use remote handling tools like tongs to keep sources far from hands.
**Shielding**: Place physical barriers between the source and workers (e.g., lead aprons, lead-lined glass windows, concrete thick walls).
Sources are always stored securely in labelled, thick lead containers when not in active use.

callouts.p: Doubling your distance from a point source reduces radiation intensity by a factor of 4 ($1/r^2$). Distance is often the most effective protection.

core.p: Radioisotopes are used inside the human body as medical tracers to monitor organ function and diagnose medical conditions without invasive surgery.
bullets: A radioactive isotope is introduced into the body, usually by injection, ingestion, or inhalation.
The tracer concentrates in specific organs or tissues depending on its chemical properties.
Gamma-emitting isotopes are essential for tracers because gamma rays can easily penetrate body tissue to be detected externally by gamma cameras.
Tracers must have a **short half-life** so they remain active long enough for the diagnostic procedure to take place, but decay quickly afterwards to minimise patient radiation dose.

callouts.p: Diagnostic tracers must emit **gamma** or **beta** radiation (gamma is most common) and have a short half-life of hours, never alpha (too ionising and blocked by skin).

core.p: High doses of ionising radiation are deliberately targeted at cancerous tumours to destroy malignant cells and shrink growths.
bullets: **External radiotherapy**: High-energy gamma rays or X-ray beams are directed at the tumour from outside the body. The machine is rotated around the patient so healthy tissue receives less dose while the tumour gets a continuous high dose.
**Internal radiotherapy (Brachytherapy)**: Small radioactive seeds or wires are placed directly inside or next to the tumour.
The goal is to deliver a lethal radiation dose to cancer cells while sparing surrounding healthy tissue as much as possible.

callouts.p: Make sure you distinguish between tracers (low dose, diagnostic, internal) and radiotherapy (high dose, treatment, curative).

core.p: Radioactive decay is random, but statistical analysis allows us to predict the time it takes for a sample's activity to decrease by half.
bullets: **Half-life** is defined as the time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample to decrease by half, OR the time taken for the activity of a source to fall to half of its initial value.
Activity is measured in **becquerels (Bq)**, where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
Different isotopes have half-lives ranging from fractions of a microsecond to billions of years.
The rate of radioactive decay is completely unaffected by external physical conditions such as temperature, pressure, or chemical bonding.

callouts.p: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for the activity of that isotope to halve.

core.p: Students must be able to calculate half-lives and remaining activities using straightforward sequential halving or graphical methods.
bullets: To find activity after $n$ half-lives: $\text{New Activity} = \text{Initial Activity} \times (1/2)^n$.
To find the number of half-lives elapsed: divide total time elapsed by the half-life ($n = t / t_{1/2}$).
When using decay curves, always draw clear construction lines from the vertical axis (activity) across to the curve, then down to the horizontal axis (time).

callouts.p: If activity drops from 800 Bq to 100 Bq, do not guess: 800 -> 400 (1) -> 200 (2) -> 100 (3). Exactly 3 half-lives have passed.

core.p: Graph analysis requires extracting half-life values from curves that level off or show logarithmic decay characteristics.
bullets: Select an easy starting activity on the y-axis (e.g., 100 Bq), find the corresponding time on the x-axis.
Find half that activity value (50 Bq) on the y-axis, follow across to the curve, and drop down to the x-axis.
Subtract the first time from the second time to find one half-life.
Repeat this for subsequent drops (e.g., 50 to 25 Bq) to check that the half-life is constant, confirming exponential decay.

callouts.p: Do not assume the decay curve reaches zero activity on the axis. Exponential curves approach zero asymptotically but never actually touch the axis.

core.p: Every day, humans are exposed to a low level of background ionising radiation originating from natural and man-made sources.
bullets: **Natural sources**: Cosmic rays from space, rocks and soil containing radioactive elements like radon gas and granite, and food/drink containing potassium-40.
**Man-made sources**: Medical procedures (X-rays, CT scans, tracer injections), nuclear power fallout, and historical weapons testing.
**Radon gas** is typically the largest contributor to natural background radiation in the UK, seeping out of uranium-bearing rocks into buildings.
When taking experimental readings with a Geiger-Muller tube, background radiation must always be measured and subtracted from the gross count rate to find the corrected count rate.

callouts.p: Background radiation is the constant, low-level ionising radiation present in the environment from natural and artificial sources.

core.p: The choice of radioactive isotope for a specific medical task depends on its half-life, type of radiation emitted, and chemical toxicity.
bullets: **Tracers**: Must emit gamma or beta radiation so it penetrates tissue to escape the body. Must have a short half-life (hours) so it decays quickly after the scan.
**Radiotherapy**: Must emit high-energy radiation (gamma or beta) capable of destroying cancer cells. Can be delivered externally or via sealed implants.
**Sterilisation**: Uses strong gamma emitters with relatively long half-lives (like Cobalt-60) so the equipment doesn't need frequent source replacement.

analogy.t: The Sizzling Popcorn Analogy for Half-Life
analogy.p: Imagine a pan of popping corn kernels on a hot stove. Each individual kernel pops (decays) at a completely random, unpredictable moment; you cannot tell which kernel will pop next. However, looking at the whole pan, it takes a very predictable amount of time (the half-life) for exactly half of the unpopped kernels to pop. Where the analogy breaks down: radioactive decay is strictly exponential and unaffected by external heat, whereas popcorn popping rate speeds up as the pan gets hotter.

terms.d: The time taken for the activity of a radioactive isotope to decrease to half its initial value.
The process of exposing an object to ionising radiation without making it radioactive.
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside materials.
The low-level ionising radiation present constantly in the environment.
The unit of radioactive activity, equal to one radioactive decay per second.
A radioactive isotope injected or ingested to track organ function.
The treatment of disease, especially cancer, using targeted doses of ionising radiation.
The process of adding or removing electrons from atoms to form charged ions.
A helium nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons.
A high-speed electron emitted from an unstable atomic nucleus.
A high-frequency electromagnetic wave emitted from a radioactive nucleus.
The measured count rate minus the background count rate.

mistakes.w: Stating that irradiation makes an object radioactive.
mistakes.r: Irradiation only exposes an object to radiation; the object does not become radioactive.

mistakes.w: Saying half-life is the time for activity to drop to zero.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for activity to drop by half, not to zero.

mistakes.w: Confusing contamination with irradiation.
mistakes.r: Contamination means radioactive atoms are physically present on or inside the material.

mistakes.w: Claiming radioactive decay rate can be slowed down by cooling the source.
mistakes.r: Radioactive decay is entirely random and unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical changes.

mistakes.w: Using alpha emitters as medical tracers inside the body.
mistakes.r: Alpha radiation is too highly ionising and cannot penetrate out of the body to be detected.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to subtract background radiation in count rate calculations.
mistakes.r: Always subtract the background count rate to get the true activity of the source.

exam.q: Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination.
model: Irradiation is exposure to radiation without physical contact with the source.
Irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
Contamination is the transfer of radioactive material onto or into an object, making it radioactive.
exam.tip: Make sure you explicitly state that only contamination results in radioactive material being present on or inside the object.

exam.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 4 hours. Its initial activity is 640 Bq. Calculate its activity after 12 hours.
model: Number of half-lives = 12 hours / 4 hours = 3 half-lives.
Activity = 640 x (1/2)^3 = 80 Bq.
exam.tip: Always calculate the number of half-lives first by dividing total time by half-life time.

exam.q: Explain why a medical tracer used inside the body must emit gamma radiation and have a short half-life.
model: Gamma radiation is highly penetrating so it can escape the body to be detected by external cameras.
Gamma is weakly ionising so it causes minimal damage to internal tissues.
A short half-life ensures the isotope decays quickly after the procedure.
This minimizes the radiation dose and harm to the patient.
exam.tip: Link every property mentioned (gamma, short half-life) directly to patient safety or detection.

exam.q: Give two natural sources of background radiation.
model: Cosmic rays from space.
Rocks and soil / Radon gas from uranium decay.
exam.tip: Keep answers concise: rocks, cosmic rays, food, and radon are standard accepted answers.

exam.q: Describe the precautions a technician must take when handling a gamma-emitting radioactive source.
model: Use long-term handling tools or tongs to keep distance from hands.
Minimize the time spent near the source.
Keep the source in a lead-lined container when not in use / use lead shielding.
exam.tip: Remember the three golden rules of radiation safety: time, distance, shielding.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term 'half-life'.
model: The time taken for the activity of a radioactive source to decrease by half.
Or: the time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample to halve.
exam.tip: Learn this definition word for word as it appears directly in mark schemes.

exam.q: Explain how ionising radiation damages living cells.
model: Radiation ionises atoms in cells by removing electrons.
This breaks chemical bonds and damages DNA, causing cell mutation or death.
exam.tip: Mention ionisation and DNA damage to secure both marks.

exam.q: A student measures a background count rate of 25 counts per minute. When a source is placed near the detector, the count rate is 225 counts per minute. What is the corrected count rate?
model: Corrected count rate = Total count rate - Background count rate.
225 - 25 = 200 counts per minute.
exam.tip: Always subtract background from the gross reading.

exam.q: Why can alpha radiation be stopped by a few centimetres of air?
model: Alpha particles have a high mass and charge.
They strongly interact with air molecules, causing rapid ionisation and losing energy quickly.
exam.tip: Connect high ionising power directly to short range.

exam.q: State why radioactive decay is described as a random process.
model: It is impossible to predict when an individual nucleus will decay.
exam.tip: One clear sentence about unpredictability gets the mark.

worked.q: A sample of iodine-131 has an initial activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 8 days. Calculate the time taken for its activity to fall to 50 Bq.
steps: Step 1: Determine how many halvings are required by dividing the activity by 2 repeatedly until reaching 50 Bq. 800 -> 400 (1) -> 200 (2) -> 100 (3) -> 50 (4).
Step 2: Note that exactly 4 half-lives have elapsed.
Step 3: Multiply the number of half-lives by the duration of one half-life: 4 x 8 days = 32 days.

worked.q: A Geiger counter records a total count rate of 340 counts per minute from a radioactive rock. The local background radiation is 40 counts per minute. If the rock's half-life is 3 hours, what will the corrected count rate be after 6 hours?
steps: Step 1: Calculate the initial corrected count rate by subtracting background: 340 - 40 = 300 counts per minute.
Step 2: Calculate how many half-lives pass in 6 hours: 6 hours / 3 hours = 2 half-lives.
Step 3: Apply the half-lives to the initial corrected count rate: 300 -> 150 -> 75 counts per minute.
